title: Mahaparinirvana Sutra, Part 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Pali Mahaparinirvana Sutra, number sixteen in the Long Discourses, and sets it beside the far longer Mahayana Nirvana Sutra, in which the Buddha never dies. Norman follows the Buddha's last tour, where the same short teaching on morality, concentration, and wisdom is repeated in every town, and describes how shabby conduct makes a person jittery, like the jewel thief in a Dustin Hoffman movie. The courtesan Ambapali crashes her chariot into the Licchavis to keep the Buddha's meal invitation, and Ananda receives the mirror of Dharma in place of more answers about the dead. Norman ends with the Buddha's instruction to Ananda to be islands unto yourselves.

sentences.text: I think today there are some new people who have arrived.
Yes.
Sorry, I don't feel like talking loud; I just feel like whispering.
Welcome to the new folks.
We didn't get a chance to say goodbye to all those who left, but in a sense, we're thanking them for their practice and thanks to you guys for showing up and giving us new strength.
We appreciate it.
Anyway, I want to talk about the Mahaparinirvana Sutra.
This sutra is about fifty pages long.
I think it's the longest sutra in the Pali canon.
There is one division of the Pali canon called Diganikaya, the long discourses, and this is in that collection, number sixteen, in the long discourses, and it's the longest of the long discourses.
It is about the last months of the Buddha's life, including his passing into nirvana.
It happens that there is another sutra which is also called the Mahaparinirvana Sutra, although usually when it is referred to, it is just referred to as the Nirvana Sutra.
This one is far longer; it is maybe, I don't know, more than a thousand pages long.
It is in several volumes, three or four volumes.
It is also about the Buddha's last months and passing into nirvana, but it is a Mahayana Sutra, which is why it is so long.
Mahayana Sutras, as you know, are really long and extravagant and outrageous.
In fact, they call them, technically, the Vaipulya Sutras.
Vaipulya means like extended or vast.
The idea is that the teachings were set forth by the Buddha, initially, very simply, with much suggestion, but not a lot being explicit.

Later, when people were warmed up to the Dharma, the Buddha went into vastly more detail to bring out the fullness of the teachings that were in the beginning, really almost like secretly embedded in the short early texts.
In reality, though, I think the Mahayana Sutras don't give you so much detail as poetry and extravagance and cosmic settings and paraphernalia and stuff.
Along the way, they do reinterpret and expand on the meanings of the earlier Pali texts.
In the Pali Mahaparinvanasutra, the Buddha gets sick and maybe bad food or something and quietly passes away.
In the Mahayana version, it takes many volumes for the Buddha to do this, but he doesn't pass away.
He explains that there is no passing away, that the Buddha is eternal.
Nothing comes, nothing goes.
There is no passing away; the Buddha is always present.

Maybe later on, if I can get around to it, I can quote you a few pages from the Nirvana Sutra to give you a flavor of what that's like, but what I really want to concentrate on in my Dharma talks is the earlier text.
It begins with King Ajata Satu of Magadha deciding that what he would really like to do is conquer the Vajras.
He says, what I would like to do is I would like to destroy them.
I would like to bring them to ruin and destruction.
So he descends an emissary to the Buddha to ask for his advice on this subject.
The emissary shows up to the Buddha, and the Buddha responds to him by asking a series of questions about the Vajras.
He receives answers to all these questions and learns that the Vajras, because he is asking very specific questions about them, are on the whole a pretty fair and reasonable people.
They meet frequently and peacefully in council.
They honor their past; they are aware of their past and they honor it.
They honor their elders of the community.
They honor their religious leaders.
They don't do cruel things to women, that is specifically mentioned.
Because of all these things, probably they will be hard to conquer because they have a just and peaceful society.
The emissary hears all this and goes away thinking to himself, well maybe we won't try to conquer the Vajras.
Instead, we will use propaganda to turn them against one another and weaken them so that they have so much dissension among them that later we will be able to conquer.
That is the take-home message that the emissary leaves with.
The Buddha, having had that conversation with the emissary of the King of Magadha, gives him an idea.
He assembles the community together and talks to them about communal harmony and what it would take for the Sangha to continue and to thrive.
He gives them many, many lists of things that they should do to that end.

Mostly, they amount to that they should meet together frequently and in harmony; that they should respect their elders; that they should respect their tradition and the past; that they should be firm in their practice; that they should keep the monastic rule; that they shouldn't have too many desires, and so on—many lists of things he tells them.

I am guessing that maybe since up until that time the Buddha was always around and could be dependent to be around, nobody had any particular reflection about how the Sangha would survive and prosper in the future.
But now that the Buddha is getting old and he knows that he is not long for this world, he is interested now in giving advice about how to go on after he is no longer around.
After he has this meeting with the Sangha, he then goes traveling here and there, as he always did, to many, many different places.
And everywhere he goes, he gives the same Dharma talk.
This Dharma talk is repeated word for word, maybe fifteen, twenty times or more, I don't know how many times in the Sutra, because wherever he goes, he gives this talk.
Here is the talk.
He says, and I am quoting from the Sutra, he says, *This is morality.
This is concentration.
This is wisdom.
Concentration, when imbued with morality, brings great fruit and profit.
Wisdom, when imbued with concentration, brings great fruit and profit.
The mind imbued with wisdom becomes free from the corruptions.
That is, from the corruption of sensuality, of becoming, of false views, and of ignorance.* And that is it.
That is the Dharma talk that he gave over and over again.
I am guessing he said more than just those words.
Those words are kind of like an outline of what he said, but that is what he said, according to the part of Anasutra, over and over again, wherever he went on this last tour of his.

Those of you who are just arriving, I will tell you that the last several days we have been talking about morality, about the three pure precepts, from Dogen's point of view, the expanded and vast point of view.
Here we have the short version.
The trouble with immorality, or shabby morality, with not paying attention to how you do things, not caring about other people, cutting corners and all that.
The trouble with all that is that it makes you nervous.
At least the Buddha thought this; that funky moral conduct makes a person nervous.
He must have seen this, he must have observed this in people of his day, and he must have observed it in himself.
I remember once I saw a really great movie starring Dustin Hoffman.
I wish I could remember the name of this movie.
It was really good.
He was played a thief in this movie, like a jewel thief.
It was a tremendous performance, very real.
This thief was a very intense, hyper-focused, jittery person.
Always pushing the limits, pushing, pushing, pushing, as if he was compelled; he couldn't stop himself.
He would always push so far that he'd get caught, and he'd go to jail a number of times in the movie.
I will never forget there was one scene which was, in fact, him robbing a jewelry store.
It was so tense and intense that you could hardly watch it; you couldn't stand to watch it.
It made you so jittery and nervous.

Later on, I found out that this movie, the screenplay for this movie was written by a novelist who wrote a novel, that the movie, the screenplay was adapted from this novel, and that this guy actually was a crook.
He actually was a jewel thief, and he actually did go to jail a number of times.

Somehow, he eventually figured out that he could make more money writing books about being a crook than being a crook, and then nobody would put him in jail probably, at least in the United States anyway, for writing a book.
So it was a better deal for him.
But no wonder the book was so real, because he really knew what he was talking about.
Maybe it is still true today that not being a person who practices ethical conduct does make you nervous and tense and jittery and under-compulsion.
Even if you never thought about being ethical, even if you don't care about it, still a certain degree of dishonesty really does make you tense.
It casts shadows in your mind, and it becomes difficult to speak or act or think or feel in a straightforward way because you are all wound up.
Your conduct kind of winds you up.
The assumption here is that a human being naturally wants to do and be good; we are born that way.
But then something goes haywire, as it often does, and then you end up not being too good.
You end up not even knowing that you would like to be good.
You end up not thinking about doing good.

Maybe you willfully don't want to be good, and you are doing lots of terrible things, which makes you an upset, nervous person, kind of messed up inside, even though it might not look like it on the outside, and maybe you yourself don't even know that.
That is what is really going on because deep inside, the way you are being goes against your deepest human nature.
That is what I think the assumption here is, and that is what the Buddha seemed to think.
In other words, he had a lot of faith in humanity, which is, I think, a good idea.
I would recommend to everyone here that you have faith in humanity, despite much evidence to the contrary.
I think it is a good thing to have faith in humanity, mostly because you yourself are a human being.
If you don't have faith in humanity, you really don't have faith in yourself, and that is hard to live with.
The Buddha thought that all sentient beings have Buddha nature.
He did not see himself as unique, at least, so it says in the Nirvana Sutra, not this Pali text, but in the Nirvana Sutra it says that.
The point that the Buddha was making in these many, many, many Dharma talks is that in order to meditate, you have to calm down.
You have to clarify that inner twitch that is brought about by funky conduct.
You have to be straightforward and clear-headed.
You have to be able to face your own pain and your own confusion, which is really the source of all immoral conduct.
Not run away from it or act it out, as we so often do.
In order to do that, you have to have a strong practice of moral conduct, which means the ability to face your own shadows and your pain.
This is not easy, and no wonder people don't want to do it.
This is why it is impossible for crooks, as crooks, as long as they keep being crooks, to do Buddhist meditation.
Maybe they can do, like, crook meditation, or some other kind of meditation, but they really cannot do Buddhist meditation, which, here the Buddha is saying, must be imbued with morality.
This is the nature of the meditation that practice that the Buddha is offering to people; it is imbued with morality.
It is not just concentration, laser focus.
The crook could have, like, laser focus.
In fact, the crook better have laser focus; you would be a lousy crook unless you really have strong focus.

No, Buddhist meditation is imbued with goodness, it is imbued with kindness, with caring, with unselfishness, with this capacity that I am saying to courageously face the pain of what has happened to us.
When concentration is imbued with these qualities, then it becomes soulful and true, and it will then, in turn, imbue wisdom with those qualities.

When wisdom is imbued with this kind of concentration, that is, when a wise and kind heart now has some depth and some strength to it, beyond the personal, beyond the emotions and the intelligence, then, as he says, this mind will be free from the corruptions of sensuality and becoming of false views and of ignorance.
And this is freedom; this is awakening, according to the Buddha.
The mind is free from the corruption of sensuality, meaning that the heart can appreciate the senses in the world without becoming enslaved by it.
The Buddha seemed to have some intuitive insight into the addictive personality.
He thought that most human beings were addicted; almost everybody thought was addicted to something or other.
These days, this seems all too true.
Almost everybody really is addicted to something, compelled by some desire or need for this or that, if not substances.
And as we know, huge numbers of people are addicted to substances, but if not substances, then maybe they are addicted to information or entertainment.
Maybe people are addicted to their own pain.
That happens; we get addicted to our own pain, our own suffering, our own dramas.
We want more and more, even as we think we want less and less.
To be free of the corruption of sensuality is to overcome our sensual and emotional predictions, to be able to safely and pleasantly enjoy our life in the world as it is.
Second, we become free of becoming, free of becoming.
This means free of the need, which is so common, we affirm it, this need to be more, have more, understand more, know more.
In other words, to be free of our constant nagging discontent.
The human mind is amazing.
It can imagine what isn't so, and it can be so focused on what isn't so that it makes what is so unsatisfactory.
When it is too hot, we think it could be cooler; there must be a way.
Maybe we can invent air conditioning; it could be cooler.
When the body is old, it imagines being younger.
I used to be able to do that.
The mind can imagine all these things.
It can be completely enamored with the idea that things could be different; things could be otherwise than as they are.
We could become something more; we could become happier people.
We could become more healthy; we could become this; we could become that; we could become smarter.
But when the mind is imbued with the kind of wisdom that the Buddha is referring to here, we would overcome that and we would be free.
Free to be as we are and be fully content and appreciative and amazed by the beauty of that.
Finally, the mind imbued with this special kind of wisdom is free of false views and ignorance.

The entire setup of conceptions and viewpoints that we do not even know we have and that tyrannize us and make us miserable people, get us to be mad at one another all the time, shocked and dismayed at the condition of the world.
We would be free of all that too.
Especially, we would be free of the deep-seated ignorance that leads us to believe that what is impermanent is not impermanent.
That what does not exist as we think it does, does exist as we think it does.
Free from false views and ignorance, we can actually love the world just as it is.
We can be just as we are without that extra added measure of toxic confusion that is so much a part of every single day of our lives and every single thought in our minds.
More or less, that is the Dharma talk that the Buddha went around giving everybody, time after time after time.
At Pata Ligama, the Buddha gave a teaching about the five disadvantages of not practicing ethical conduct.
In these last months of his life, he was very much thinking about ethical conduct.
Do you want to know the five disadvantages?

Not that anybody here is not practicing ethical conduct, but in case anybody asks you what the five disadvantages of ethical conduct are, I will tell you what the Buddha thought about that in these months of his life.
Here are the five disadvantages of not practicing ethical conduct.
First of all, you will not be prosperous because you are not honestly taking care of things, you know, paying your bills on time and whatnot.
Maybe you are doing tricky deals of various sorts or you are over-leveraged.
or you're running around, doing too many deals all the time, and you won't be prosperous.
Second, you will be known as an immoral person, so you'll have a crappy reputation.
People won't think highly of you, and that'll be a source of trouble for you.
Third, and this is an interesting one, not practicing morality will make you paranoid of people.
You'll always be wary that somebody's going to find you out, and you won't even know necessarily; you feel that maybe you have a kind of sense of wariness.
Whenever you're around people, you'll be wary.
You'll either have to be false, brash, and outrageous to cover it up, or you'll just be like a scared, nervous person always looking over your shoulder.
That's the third disadvantage of not practicing morality.
The fourth one is that when you die, you're going to be a wreck.
You're going to be terrified, freaked out.
It's not going to be pretty when you die.
And the fifth one is that after you die, it'll be even worse.
So, these should give us incentive to practice morality.
At Kottegama, where he went next, he gave the usual Donna talk.
But before he gave that talk, he mentioned, again, the Four Noble Truths.
He mentioned the Four Noble Truths in his first Donna talk, forty-five years earlier.
And here, forty-five years later, he speaks of them again.
I wonder how many times he repeated in various ways the Four Noble Truths in forty-five years.
How many times?
How many thousands and thousands of times did he speak about the Four Noble Truths?
And here, again, he speaks of them with full conviction and passion.
He's always traveling with Ananda, and so now there's a little funny episode.
I think it's funny, anyway, with Ananda.
They were staying at the Brick House at Nanika.
In the evening, Ananda was saying, a lot of people have died lately in the Sangha.
And I wonder what is the fate of all these people who have died.
He lists a whole bunch of different people who have died.
He says, "Would you tell me, Buddha, because Buddha is clairvoyant and knows everything, would you tell me what is happening?
What is the fate of all these people?"
So the Buddha goes down the list and he tells what's happening to everyone.
This one is an arhat and has already entered Parinirvana.
This one is just about an inch away from that.
In the in-between world after death, she will probably be taken care of and she'll be fine.
This one here will have to come back for one more lifetime.
This one maybe a couple of lifetimes.
And he goes down the list and tells the fate of each one of these people.
At the end of all this, he says to Ananda, "This is getting tiresome, having to tell you about all this stuff.
What are you going to do when I'm not around to be telling you about all this stuff?
So now I'm going to tell you about the mirror of Dharma.
With this mirror of Dharma, all you have to do is look in the mirror of Dharma and you'll be able to tell what your spiritual condition is.
And you won't need me to be answering all these tiresome questions anymore."
So then he explains to Ananda the mirror of Dharma.
And there are four elements to the mirror of Dharma.
So all you have to do is assess yourself on these four elements and you'll know.
First, unwavering confidence in the Buddha, which means Buddha nature—unwavering confidence in the possibility that all human beings have the capacity for awakening, including you.
That's the first element of the Dharma mirror.
The second is unwavering confidence in the Dharma, that there is in fact a way to practice and understand your life that will lead to awakening.

Third, unwavering confidence in the Sangha, that there actually are in this world of imperfect people, more or less trustworthy people who actually are trying to live in the world, who do have faith in the Buddha, do live the Dharma, do cooperate with one another and will support you.
And that furthermore, all beings support you.
Having confidence in the Sangha is the third element of the Dharma mirror.

And the fourth one is that the person would practice ethical conduct, would not be willfully selfish, would not be doing harm to others, would in other words refrain from evil, do good and purify the mind.
They went to Vesali, where they stayed in the grove of Ambapali, who was a courtesan.
She had a park and they camped there.
And there he gave a discourse, the Buddha gave a discourse about mindfulness, in which he said more or less, "Pay attention.
Pay attention to your body, to feelings, to perceptions, to impulses, to awareness itself, to thoughts, to feelings, to Dharmas.
Forget about making progress, forget about being a hero, forget about saving the world, forget about being rich or good looking or healthy.
Just devote yourself to paying attention.

Pay attention to walking forward, pay attention to walking backward, pay attention to lifting something up, pay attention to putting something down, pay attention to your robe, pay attention to your bowl, pay attention to eating, drinking, chewing, swallowing, tasting, pay attention to pissing and shitting."
He says, "Pay attention to pissing and shitting.
Pay attention when you're sitting, when you're walking, when you're standing, when you're lying down, pay attention when you're speaking, pay attention when you're silent.
Pay attention."
That's what he told them.
Now comes another funny story about this Ambapali, the courtesan.
What is a courtesan, anyway?
Basically a high-class prostitute, right, more or less, like a kept woman in the court.
So in a lot of high cultures, there was a whole group, a class of courtesans.
They are in a sort of funny ambiguous position because they move among the exclusive high classes and yet they're not really of those classes.
So Buddha camped in her grove.
So Ambapali comes in her chariot to visit the Buddha and she invites him for a meal and he agrees to come.
He always agreed to come to a meal by saying nothing.
That was the way he agreed.
When they said, "Would you come to the meal?" and the Buddha didn't say anything, they understood, "Oh, he's coming."
So that's what happened.
So she was very excited.
She must have thought, "Wow, on a courtesan, he's coming to a meal with me.
Oh, that's great."
So she charges away in a chariot really happy about this.

And as she's leaving the camp, these guys called the Luchavi, who I think must have been from the contacts we gathered, they were very important people in this region, much more important people in this courtesan.
They heard that the Buddha was around and described how they got all dolled up.
They got out their best chariots and they put on their best clothing and they put on a fancy blue and red makeup.
I guess guys wore makeup in ancient India at all.
They probably came looking like, in fact when they came, the Buddha said, "Look, the gods from the thirty-three heavens are coming.
They look so amazing."
So they're off going to the Buddhist place, right, and Ambapali is down the road in the other direction.
And she, it seems like, it doesn't say exactly, but it seems like she on purpose like runs right into them, like smashes into them.
What it says is she met them axle to axle, wheel to wheel, yoke to yoke.
She basically crashed into them on purpose, on purpose, very proudly, very happily.
I think she probably had dealings with them in the past and she was very happy to let them know, "Guess who's coming to my house?"
And they said, "We will give you one hundred thousand pieces of gold."
Courtesans like money.
That's what they do.
They take money for favors.
"We will offer you one hundred thousand pieces of gold if you will let the Buddha come to my house for dinner, our house for dinner."
And she says, "Absolutely no way.
There is no way."
And they say, "Damn, defeated by a stupid courtesan."
But they figure, you know, the Buddha will solve this for them.
So they go on into the camp.

She goes home, I guess, and they go on into the camp and they proudly stride up to the Buddha and they invite the Buddha for the meal, figuring that the Buddha's not going to go have dinner with the courtesan when he could have me having the meal with the Luchawis, not dinner, but the meal.
So the Buddha says, "Oh, I'm sorry.
I would love to do that, but I'm already committed to going somewhere else for the meal."
They say, "Damn, defeated by a stupid courtesan."
So in the Pali Sutta, stuff like this happens from time to time because these Suttas are a little bit realistic.
They're not one hundred percent idealistic.
Mayana Sutras, on the other hand, are one hundred fifty percent idealistic.
So stuff like this never happens in Mayana Sutras.

But, yes, we can imagine, and the Sutra very honestly reminds us that yes, even in the presence of the Buddha, there was jealousy and people were using their relationships to the Buddha to maybe take out their aggressiveness, aggressions on one another to increase their prestige, or maybe just their own personal self-satisfaction.
Because people are always people, right?
People are always going to be people, with the sole exception of in the Mayana Sutras.
So, just like now, then too, there were all sorts of rivalries and jealousies and misunderstandings and troubles.
And even the Buddha did not have the magical power to cause this not to be the case.
The Buddha seemed not to have noticed all this that much.
He was aware of it.
Once in a while, there's a mention of him getting a bit fed up with it.
But mostly, he didn't really think about it or notice it.
He, in general, didn't try to straighten people out and tell them what to do and not to do, what to be and how not to be.
He mostly shared his practice, offered the Dharma as he saw it.
And he figured that the rest is up to people.
He didn't seem over-worried about this stuff.
Anyway, as it says in the Sutra, he stayed at the Grove of Ambapali as long as he felt like it.
It doesn't say exactly how long, but as long as he wanted to stay.
And then he left.
And he went to Beluva where they were going to spend the rains season.
Now I'll quote from the text.
"Then it occurred to the Blessed One.
So it came about that the Blessed One's illness was allayed, and he recovered.
And soon after his recovery, he came out from his dwelling place and sat down in the shade of the building on a seat prepared for him.

Then the Venerable Ananda approached the Blessed One, respectfully greeted him, and sitting down at one side, he spoke to the Blessed One, saying, 'Fortunate it is for me, O Lord, to see the Blessed One at ease again.
Fortunate it is for me, O Lord, to see the Blessed One recovered.
For truly, Lord, when I saw the Blessed One's sickness, it was as though my own body became weak as a creeper, and everything around became dim to me, and my senses failed me.

And yet, I still had some little comfort in the thought that the Blessed One would not come to his final passing away until he had given some last instructions respecting the community of Bhikkhus.' Thus spoke the Venerable Ananda, but the Blessed One answered him, saying,"
"What more does the community of Bhikkhus expect from me, Ananda?
I have set forth the Dhamma without making any distinction of esoteric and exoteric doctrine.
There is nothing, Ananda, with regard to the teachings that the Tathagata holds to the last with a closed fist of a teacher who keeps something back.
I've given everything.
What more could you want?
Whosoever may think that it is he or she who should lead the community of Bhikkhus or Bhikkhunis, or that the community depends on him or her, let that person give last instructions.
But, Ananda, the Tathagata has no such idea.
I, the Buddha, have no such idea that it is he who should lead the community of Bhikkhus or that the community depends on him.
So what instructions should he have to give regarding the community of Bhikkhus?
So, we suppose that leaders of communities should take these words to heart and find comfort in them."

If the Buddha didn't think he was the leader of the community, or that the community depended on him, or that he was expected to give instructions to the community and straighten everybody out, then why should we think that we're supposed to do all that?

We should imitate the Buddha and just practice with people for forty-five or fifty years the best we can, be willing to be completely open with everything, holding nothing back, any way to be as thorough as we can be in sharing our life with others.
And then when it's time to stop, we should just stop trusting that all will be well.
The Buddha went on, "Now I am frail, Ananda, old, aged, far gone in years.
This is my eighty-fifth year.
Doesn't seem that old to me, but oh well, he thought he was old.
Eighty-five's not that old, right?
People around here have mothers who are ninety-nine, ninety-seven."
But the Buddha was only eighty, a mere child.
But he thought he was old, I guess maybe in those days.
"This is my eighty-fifth year, and my life is spent.
Even as an old cart, Ananda, is held together with much difficulty.
So the body of the Tathagata is kept going only with supports, like I'm strapped together with duct tape, and what do you call those things, bungee cords.
That's what it's like to be me.
Ananda, when I'm disregarding external objects, only with the cessation of certain feelings, only when I attain to and abide in the signless concentration of mind, is my body finally comfortable."
"Therefore, Ananda, be islands unto yourselves.
Be refuges unto yourselves, seeking no external refuge.
With the Dharma as your island, with the Dharma as your refuge, seeking no other refuge.
So I'll stop there."
There's still a long way to go before the Buddha's passing.
I'm selecting parts that I think are interesting.
We'll see how far we get.
So one short final note before we part company for now.

Maybe you know that while we've been sitting here this week, there's been a great roar of public outcry from all around the world about this separation of the immigrant families, children from their parents that Tim talked about on the first day.
Drumbeat of upset about this gets louder and louder.

And now, just today, the President of the United States says, as he often vaguely says, that he will sign something or other, I think that's his actual quote, that he will sign something or other very soon to make the situation better.
So we don't know what this means, but it means that it can't go on as it was.
This is unsustainable to keep going with this kind of policy.
So something or other will change.
And if I find something out about it between now and the time that I speak to you tomorrow morning, I will let you know.
I hear that because Tim brought to our attention, and we've been sitting with it even if we haven't been thinking about it directly.
It's been in our hearts, I know.
But let's do, please, maintain silence and stability.
Let's not be looking at our phones and following in who will let you know if something is worth knowing.
Let us continue to maintain the integrity of our session.
It's very important, especially at this time in the session, that we keep silence.
We're not talking to one another.
Keep the practice going strongly.
Our sitting is doubtless a part of what the world needs to right itself.
So this week, this is our responsibility.
This is what we have to take care of.
So let's be sure to do that.
Thank you very much for listening.

verbatim.text: I think today there are some new people who have arrived, right? Yes. Yes, sorry. I don't feel like talking loud. I just feel like whispering. Welcome to the new folks.
